title: Multiplexed streaming penumbra — client-side notebook
body:
Goal:
Small notebook to capture experiments on how client-side multiplexing (HTTP/2 streams + gRPC) interacts with server-side streaming and prefix/KV cache behavior. Nicknamed 'penumbra' because the bad tail lives in the shadow between transport multiplexing and runtime queueing.

Hypothesis:
- When many small streaming responses are multiplexed over a few long-lived connections, we see elevated p95/p99 vs the same RPS with one-request-per-connection. Suspect interaction of runtime request scheduling, per-connection flow-control windows, and async writeback stalls.

Environment:
- Dedicated test cluster: 2x A100s, 48 vCPU, 512GB RAM (dev pool, dedicated-sim).
- Model: redwood/compact-chat-gt2 (sequence 512 typical).
- Runtime: bench image built from commit ab12cd3 (bench-harness PR linked).
- Edge: envoy-proxy (http/2 enabled) fronting runtime on port 8443.

Client harness:
- custom harness (bench-harness) that can run two modes: "single-conn-per-request" and "few-connections-multiplexed".
- typical client config used: 100 clients, 10 connections each in multiplexed mode (so 1000 streams max concurrently), payloads: 45B prompt avg, streaming token-by-token with SSE/grpc chunking.

Quick test matrix (representative runs):
ID, mode, clients, connections, target-rps, p50(ms), p95(ms), p99(ms)
A1, baseline-singleconn, 100, 1000, 800 req/s, 72, 210, 460
B2, multiplex-10conn, 100, 100, 800 req/s, 88, 380, 910
B3, multiplex-10conn, 200, 100, 1600 req/s, 140, 820, 1800
C1, multiplex-2conn, 100, 20, 800 req/s, 95, 440, 1200
D1, singleconn-coldcache, 100, 1000, 400 req/s, 120, 560, 1300

Notes on numbers: these are from short 5min runs; noisy but consistent pattern: p95/p99 grow substantially when using few-connections + many streams. p50 moves up modestly.

Telemetry looked-for:
- per-connection flow-control stalls (envoy metrics),
- runtime worker event loop latencies (trace spans),
- kernel-level send buffer full counters (netstat / ss),
- writeback retries from our async socket layer.

Observations:
- Envoy shows long-lived streams with occasional backlog on connection write bytes. When the backlog grows, small streams (short responses) get delayed behind a long streaming response's outstanding window updates.
- Runtime traces show spikes in queueing time for request-fanout when a hot connection has a blocked socket write syscall.
- Disabling HTTP/2 flow control at Envoy (workaround) reduces p99 by ~30% in small runs but is not acceptable long-term.
- Cold cache amplifies the effect because the long-running token emission holds the same connection for longer, preventing small priming requests from ever getting headroom.

Hypothesized root causes (ranked):
1) Transport-level head-of-line within connection due to small default flow-control window + long streaming responses.
2) Runtime's per-connection scheduling doesn't preempt an active streaming request quickly enough (we schedule by FIFO).
3) Backpressure propagation to accept loop causes bursts of socket-level stalls.

Immediate follow-ups / TODOs:
- Add an experiment variant where runtime interrupts streaming writes after N tokens to let other streams make progress. (task: bench-harness PR to add preemptive-yield behavior).
- Try increasing http2 initial window size in Envoy and measure delta.
- Run a microbenchmark isolating only kernel socket writeback: toy server that writes a 10KB frame continuously vs many small 200B frames multiplexed.
- Add more traces: capture full envoy->runtime frames with timestamps (will need high-cardinality sampling).
- Check TLS stack: does NSS/OpenSSL buffer behavior differ under our build? Quick check: replace with plaintext (dev only) to see difference.

Quick notes to self:
- When running long experiments, rotate logs every 1h; got a single run yesterday that hit file descriptor exhaustion due to client harness bug.
- Keep an eye on PR #132 — merging the new harness options will let me run the 'preemptive-yield' mode at scale.
- Slack thread for initial observations: #runtime-penumbra (linked).

Conclusions so far (working):
- Multiplexing over a small number of connections increases tail latencies for short streaming responses compared to single-conn-per-request, even at the same nominal RPS.
- Fix space likely spans transport (Envoy settings) and runtime scheduler modifications.
- Short-term mitigation: increase connection count per client or tune HTTP/2 window sizes; long-term: runtime preemption and smarter scheduling for streaming writes.

Experiment commands (notes / copyable):
- run harness: ./bench-harness --mode multiplex --clients 100 --conns-per-client 2 --rps 800 --streaming
- check envoy counters: curl -s http://localhost:9901/stats | grep http2.*window
- quick kernel check: ss -s && /proc/net/snmp | grep Tcp

Logged at end of run (2025-08-19 15:20 UTC): "merge candidate: preemptive-yield bench shows promising reduction in p99 (approx -28%) on 2k stream run" — needs 12h stability run.

References / links inline: bench-harness PR, linear ticket, quick trace screenshots in the PR checklist.

End of notebook entry.

-- Rowan
